Rhinosporidium seeberi and Pneumocystis jiroveci organisms that are non cultivable.

**Zygomycosis** or **Mucormycosis** is an invasive disease caused by zygomycetes principally by species of **Rhizopus, Mucor and Absidia.**

Predisposing factors for mucormycosis include **diabetes mellitus,** cancers such as lymphomas, kidney failure, and organ transplant.

• **Branched sporangiophores** along aerial mycelium is seen. Rhizoids are absent.

**Rhizopus:**

• **Rhizoids** are present and sporangiophores arise directly above the rhizoids.

**Absidia:**

• It bears internodal **rhizoids.**

**Cultural characteristics:**

• Culture on SDA reveals the appearance of white cottony woolly/fluffy colonies , initially which is similar to all the three genera.
• However, later, the colonies of rhizopus turn brown-black due to sporulation, giving rise to salt and pepper appearance .

**Mycotic poisoning** is of two types: Mycetism and Mycotoxicosis

**Mycetism:**

The fungus itself causes toxic effects

Examples:

• Claviceps → **Ergot poisoning**
• Coprine → coprine poisoning
• Inocybe → muscarine poisoning

**Mycotoxicosis:**

Fungal toxins contaminate food and causes toxic effects.

Example:

• **Aflatoxins:** These are a type of **mycotoxins** produced by *Aspergillus* species of fungi, such as *A. flavus* and *A. parasiticus.*
• **Fusarium** toxins
• **Citrinin toxin** was first isolated from *Penicillium citrinum.*

images.caption: High-power H&E photomicrograph showing a cluster of golden-brown, thick-walled, transversely septate sclerotic bodies (Medlar bodies / 'copper penny' bodies) in chromoblastomycosis
images.visual_description: High-power H&E histopathological photomicrograph showing a cluster of four golden-brown, thick-walled, round-to-polyhedral fungal cells with internal transverse septations (Medlar bodies / sclerotic bodies / 'copper pennies') surrounded by inflammatory cells.

explanation_markdown:
The given clinical history and histopathological image are suggestive of **Chromoblastomycosis**

Chromoblastomycosis (chromomycosis) is a **subcutaneous mycotic infection** that is usually caused by **traumatic inoculation.**

Over months to years, the primary lesion **becomes verrucous and wart-like** with extension along the draining lymphatics.

Histologically, the lesions are **granulomatous** and the dark sclerotic bodies may be seen within leukocytes or giant cells (**medlar/copper penny bodies**)

Other dematiaceous fungi, having melanized cell walls:

• *Phialophora verrucosa*
• *Fonsecaea pedrosoi*
• *Fonsecaea compacta*
• *Rhinocladiella aquaspersa*
• *Cladophialophora carrionii*

question_stem.text: Toxocara canis infecting humans is an example of _____
question_stem.markdown: Toxocara canis infecting humans is an example of _____

peer_accuracy_statement: 13% of the people got this right
explanation_markdown:
***Toxocara canis*** (dog roundworm) is an example of an **aberrant parasite.**

Parasites can be divided into ectoparasites and endoparasites.

• **Ectoparasites** inhabit only the body surface of the host without penetrating the tissue. The term **infestation** is often employed for parasitization with ectoparasites.
• **Endoparasite:** A parasite, which lives within the body of the host and is said to cause an infection is called an endoparasite.

Endoparasites are further classified as follows:

• Obligate parasite: Parasite which cannot exist without a host. e.g. *Toxoplasma gondii* and *Plasmodium.*
• Facultative parasite: Organisms can live as parasitic or free-living forms.
• Accidental parasite: Parasites that infect an unusual host. E.g.; *Echinococcus granulosus* infects man.
• Aberrant parasite: Parasites which infect a host where they cannot develop further. They are also known as wandering parasites. E.g.; *Toxocara canis* (dog roundworm) infecting humans.

peer_accuracy_statement: 32% of the people got this right

• **Paratenic Host:** A host in which the larval stage of the parasite remains viable without further development is referred to as a paratenic host.

**Other types** of hosts:

• **Definitive Host:** Host in which **sexual reproduction** of parasite takes place
• **Intermediate Host:** Host in which **asexual multiplication** of parasite occurs
• **Reservoir Host:** In an endemic area, the parasitic infection is kept up by the presence of a host that harbors the parasite and acts as an important source of infection to other susceptible hosts.
• **Accidental Host:** Host in which parasite is **not usually found**

**Trypanosoma gambiense** exhibits **antigenic variation** within the host. This genetic switch protects them from **antibodies.**

• *Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense*
• *Plasmodium* spp.
• *Giardia lamblia*

The following image shows the *Trypanosoma brucei.*

The *Trypanosoma brucei* cell membrane is densely packed with VSG dimers, which make up ~90% of its cell surface protein, and which allows for the parasite to evade the immune system and establish chronic infection.

• It is an **immediate hypersensitivity** (Type 1) **skin test** used in the diagnosis of **hydatid disease.**
• The **antigen in hydatid fluid** is collected from animal or human cysts and is sterilized by **Seitz or membrane filtration.**
• The **fluid** is then injected (0.2 mL) **intradermally** in one arm and an equal volume of **saline** as **control** is injected in the other arm.
• The appearance of a **large wheal of about 5 cm** in diameter with multiple pseudopodia-like projections within half an hour on the test side indicates a **positive reaction.** The wheal usually fades in about an hour.
• A **secondary reaction** consisting of **edema and induration** appears after 48 hours.
• The test is abandoned now due to non-specificity and has been supplemented by serological tests.

question_stem.text: The most common extra-intestinal complication of amoebiasis is _______
question_stem.markdown: The most common extra-intestinal complication of amoebiasis is _______

peer_accuracy_statement: 87% of the people got this right
explanation_markdown:
• **Hepatic amoebiasis** is the most common **extraintestinal complication** of amoebiasis.
• Almost most of the trophozoites reach the liver, in amoebic dysentery, however, only a small portion of them actually lodge and multiply in the liver cells.
• Several patients with amoebic colitis develop an **enlarged tender liver** without detectable impairment of liver function or fever called **amoebic hepatitis**
• In 5-10% cases of intestinal amoebiasis, liver abscesses may occur.
• The center of the abscess contains **thick chocolate brown pus (anchovy sauce pus),** which is liquefied necrotic liver tissue. It is **bacteriologically sterile** and **free of amoeba.** At the periphery, there is almost normal liver tissue, which contains invading amoeba.

**Complications and sequelae of intestinal amoebiasis**

1. **Fulminant amoebic colitis**
  ◦ Toxic megacolon
  ◦ Perianal ulceration
  ◦ Ameboma
2. **Extraintestinal amoebiasis**
  ◦ Amoebic hepatitis (most common)
  ◦ Amoebic liver abscess
  ◦ Amoebic appendicitis and peritonitis
  ◦ Pulmonary amoebiasis
  ◦ Cerebral amoebiasis
  ◦ Splenic abscess
  ◦ Cutaneous amoebiasis
  ◦ Genitourinary amoebiasis

question_stem.text: A 25-year-old patient presented with signs of meningoencephalitis following swimming in a nearby local pond one week back. The CSF on wet mount microscopy revealed motile unicellular microorganisms. The most likely organism is _______
question_stem.markdown: A 25-year-old patient presented with signs of meningoencephalitis following swimming in a nearby local pond one week back. The CSF on wet mount microscopy revealed motile unicellular microorganisms. The most likely organism is _______

peer_accuracy_statement: 76% of the people got this right
explanation_markdown:
The unicellular microorganism is most likely to be *Naegleria fowleri* also known as **"Brain eating amoeba".**

*N.fowleri* causes **Primary amoebic meningoencephalitis.**

It occurs in 3 forms: cyst, amoeboid trophozoite and flagellate trophozoite forms.

The amoebae invade the nasal mucosa and pass through the olfactory nerve branches in the cribriform plate into the meninges.

Incubation period is 2 days to 2 weeks.

• Human beings acquire by inhalation of cyst or trophozoite, ingestion of cysts, or through traumatized skin or eyes.

images.caption: Speculum examination photograph showing punctate mucosal petechial hemorrhages on the ectocervix ('strawberry cervix' / colpitis macularis) in Trichomonas vaginalis infection
images.visual_description: Clinical colposcopic/speculum photograph of the uterine cervix showing diffuse erythema studded with numerous pinpoint bright-red petechial hemorrhages ('strawberry cervix') caused by Trichomonas vaginalis.

explanation_markdown:
*Trichomonas vaginalis* is the only protozoa with one stage in its life cycle with **only Trophozoite form** (No cyst stage is seen).

It is an **obligate parasite** and cannot live without close association with vaginal, urethral or prostatic tissues.

Culture is generally done when direct microscopy is negative. It is considered Gold standard. It is grown on solid or liquid media. **Cysteine-peptone-liver-maltose (CPLM) medium** and **Plastic envelope medium (PEM)** are often used.

**A mature schizont** contains **8-32 merozoites** and **hemozoin.** This will burst releasing merozoites into the circulation. The merozoites invade fresh erythrocytes, in which they go through the same process of development called as **erythrocytic schizogony** or **merogony.**

After the ring form is formed in peripheral blood, the remaining RBC cycle of **falciparum** occurs in the capillaries of brain and other internal organs. Hence only the ring form is seen in the **peripheral smear.**

However, for other Plasmodium species, all erythrocytic stages occur in peripheral blood vessels.

question_stem.text: Which of the following statements is true regarding Toxoplasma gondii?
question_stem.markdown: Which of the following statements is true regarding Toxoplasma gondii?

options.text: Gametogony occurs inside the human beings
Tachyzoites are formed within the definitive host
The tachyzoites inside the tissue cyst can be reactivated in immunosuppression

peer_accuracy_statement: 43% of the people got this right
explanation_markdown:
**Human toxoplasmosis is a zoonosis.**

Both **sexual reproduction (gametogony)** and asexual reproduction (schizogony) occur within the mucosal epithelial cells of the **small intestine of the cat.**

Toxoplasma gondii has two types of life cycles:

• Enteric cycle
• Exoenteric cycle

**Enteric cycle** occurs in cat and other **definitive host,** whereas **exoenteric cycle** occurs in Humans, mice, rats etc. which are the **intermediate hosts.**

**Sporozoites** from the oocysts and **bradyzoites** from the tissue cysts enter the intestinal mucosa and multiply asexually and **tachyzoites** are formed within the **intermediate host.**

**Tachyzoites** continue to multiply and spread locally by lymphatic system and blood, while the **bradyzoites** multiply slowly inside the **tissue cyst.**

The **dormant bradyzoites** inside the cyst may be **reactivated** in immune suppression causing renewed infection in the host.

explanation_markdown:
**The life cycle of Entamoeba Histolytica has 2 stages, the motile amoeba (trophozoite) and the nonmotile cyst,** which are both seen in the life cycle shown above.

The trophozoite is found within the intestinal and extraintestinal lesions and hence in diarrheal stools. The cyst predominates in non-diarrheal stools.

**Pathogenesis**

• The organism is acquired by **ingestion of cysts** that are transmitted primarily by the **fecal–oral route**
• There is **no animal reservoir**
• The ingested cysts differentiate into trophozoites in the ileum which invades the colonic epithelium
• As the lesion reaches the muscularis layer, a typical **"flask-shaped" ulcers** are formed.
• The most frequent site of systemic disease is the **liver,** with abscesses containing trophozoites.

**Clinical features**

• Acute intestinal amebiasis presents as dysentery accompanied by lower abdominal discomfort and flatulence. Stools usually have blood and mucus.
• Chronic amebiasis with low-grade symptoms such as occasional diarrhoea, weight loss, and fatigue.
• A granulomatous lesion called an **ameboma** may form in the cecal or rectosigmoid areas of the colon which can resemble an adenocarcinoma of the colon.
• **Amoebic abscess of the liver** is characterised by right-upper-quadrant pain, weight loss, fever, and a tender, enlarged liver.
• Aspiration of the liver abscess yields brownish-yellow pus with the appearance and consistency of **anchovy paste.**

• The **enzyme phosphatase** which is normally present in milk, is inactivated if pasteurisation has been performed properly.

question_stem.text: Which of the following methods of PCR can be used to quantitate the amplified product simultaneously?
question_stem.markdown: Which of the following methods of PCR can be used to quantitate the amplified product simultaneously?

peer_accuracy_statement: 51% of the people got this right
explanation_markdown:
PCR is the most widely used, target nucleic acid amplification method.

**Types of PCR:**

• **Multiplex PCR:** More than 1 primer is included. One primer is directed at sequences present in all clinically relevant bacteria and second primer is directed at a specific sequence.
• **Nested PCR:** It involves the sequential use of two primer sets. First primer set is used for amplification and the amplicon obtained is then used as a target sequence for second amplification.
• **Reverse transcriptase PCR:** It is used for **DNA synthesis** from a viral RNA template
• **Real-time PCR:** This combines nucleic acid amplification with quantitative or quantitative measurement of the amplified product.

explanation_markdown:
'**Myeloma** cells lack hypoxanthine phosphoribosyl transferase **(HGPRT)** enzyme; hence, they cannot grow well in HAT medium.'

**Hybridoma technology** is a method for producing large numbers of identical antibodies (also called monoclonal antibodies).

**Hybridomas** are somatic cell hybrids produced by fusing the antibody-forming spleen cells with myeloma cells. The resultant hybrid thus has both the antibody-producing ability of the B-cell and the ability to multiply indefinitely of the myeloma.

The following are the various steps involved in hybridoma technology:

1. **Mice are immunized** with an antigen, after several weeks of immunization, blood samples are obtained from mice for measurement of serum antibodies.
2. When the antibody titer is high enough, mice are commonly **boosted by injecting antigen** without adjuvant intraperitoneally or intravenously, then the mice are **euthanized** and their spleens removed for in vitro hybridoma cell production.
3. **Fusing antibody-producing spleen cells,** which have a limited life span with cells derived from an immortal tumor of lymphocytes **(myeloma)** results in a hybridoma that is capable of unlimited growth.
4. The **hypoxanthine, aminopterin, and thymidine (HAT)** medium allows only the fused cells to survive in culture.

question_stem.markdown: A patient admitted to an ICU is on a central venous line for the last one week. He is on ceftazidime and amikacin. After 7 days of antibiotics, he develops a spike of fever, and his blood culture is positive for gram-positive cocci in chains, which are catalase negative. Following this, vancomycin was started, but the culture remained positive for the same organism even after 2 weeks of therapy. The most likely organism causing infection is ______.

peer_accuracy_statement: 40% of the people got this right
explanation_markdown:
From the case scenario, the most likely organism involved is *Enterococcus faecalis.*

The culture is catalase negative, so *Staphylocococcus aureus* and coagulase-negative *Staphylococcus* are ruled out.

And, *Streptococcus viridians* is usually sensitive to penicillin, except in neutropenic patients where vancomycin is given; hence, it is ruled out.

So, the points are in favor of *Enterococcus faecalis.*

Here, even after treatment with aminoglycoside, cephalosporin, and even with vancomycin, the culture remains positive. So, this is a case of **vancomycin-resistant enterococci.** The mechanism is the alteration of the D-alanyl–D-alanine chain in cell wall.
